title-group.article-title: The combination of a cancer vaccine, pembrolizumab, and stereotactic body radiation in patients with locally advanced pancreatic cancer: a single-arm, phase II study

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: In this Phase II study (NCT02648282) of locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC), 58 patients were enrolled and intended for an immunotherapy including GM-CSF-secreting allogeneic pancreatic cancer vaccine (GVAX) and pembrolizumab and stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) following standard chemotherapy. Fifty-four evaluable patients received two cycles of immunotherapy and SBRT and reassessed for resectability. After resection or biopsy, patients received continued immunotherapy for two years. At a median follow-up of 19.6 months, the median distant metastasis free survival (DMFS), the primary endpoint, for all evaluable patients was 9.8 months. Secondary endpoint analysis shows that, of these, 35 patients (64.8%) were deemed potentially resectable, and 24 underwent R0/R1 resections. Resected patients had a majority of R0 resections (91.7%). The overall resection rate was 44.4%. Patients who underwent resection had a median DMFS of 20.3 months. Median overall survival (OS), a secondary endpoint, for all evaluable patients from the start of the immunotherapy was 21.8 months, with resected patients reaching 29.7 months and unresected patients at 12.1 months. From diagnosis, median OS was 28.2 months, with resected patients achieving 36.7 months, while unresected patients had 19.7 months. In conclusion, the combination of GVAX, pembrolizumab, and SBRT showed promising efficacy in LAPC patients with favorable survival outcomes, especially those who underwent R0/R1 resections. However, patients with unresectable disease still maintained significantly worse DMFS and OS. The regimen demonstrated a manageable safety profile.

sec.p: Subject terms: Pancreatic cancer, Cancer immunotherapy, Radiotherapy

abstract.p: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma carries a poor prognosis, with pancreatectomy as the only potentially curative option. This Phase II trial assessed distant metastasis-free survival in locally advanced disease using GVAX vaccine, pembrolizumab, and SBRT following chemotherapy.

sec.p: Received 2025 Apr 24; Accepted 2026 Jan 27; Collection date 2026.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The prognosis for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is dismal, and the overall 5-year survival rate for all stages at diagnosis is around 12% in the United States1. The management of PDACs requires a multidisciplinary approach that integrates multiple treatment modalities, including surgery, radiotherapy (RT), chemotherapy, and, in the clinical trial settings, emerging therapies such as immunotherapy and targeted therapy. Pancreatectomy offers the only chance of cure for pancreatic cancer. Based on the severity of the blood vessel involvement, localized pancreatic cancers are categorized into resectable pancreatic cancer, borderline resectable pancreatic cancer, and locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC). Given the aggressive nature of pancreatic cancer and the complexity of its treatment, a multimodality strategy, with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, is essential to address the disease at different stages for an improved overall survival (OS) and, with neoadjuvant RT, to further increase the chance of R0 resection. We previously reported that 20% of LAPCs treated with chemotherapy followed by stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) were successfully down-staged and underwent R0 or R1 resection2.

About 30% of the newly diagnosed PDAC cases first present as LAPC3, which is deemed surgically inoperable because of the involvement of the surrounding vasculature. The current standard treatment for LAPC is a combination of induction chemotherapy and RT, including chemoradiation or SBRT4. Compared to conventional chemoradiation, SBRT resulted in more frequent complete pathologic responses5 and reduced lymphocyte suppression in LAPCs6. Nevertheless, novel therapeutic strategies are still highly demanded to increase surgical resection rates and ultimately curability in LAPCs.

For many advanced malignancies, immunotherapies, particularly the immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), have become an alternative or additive standard of care treatment. Unfortunately, immunotherapy has demonstrated minimal therapeutic effects in PDACs7. ICIs such as anti-PD-1 or PD-L1 antibodies potentiate tumor antigen-specific effector T cells (Teffs) by reinvigorating their function. The quantity of tumor-infiltrating Teffs predicts the survival outcome in those cancer types that respond to immunotherapy, but is low in the tumor microenvironment (TME) of PDACs8. The TME in PDAC is also immunosuppressive, not only preventing T cell infiltration, but also suppressing Teff function9.

Recent studies have suggested that RT can prime the TME with Teffs by inducing immunogenic tumor cell death, which triggers innate immune responses, thus serving as an “in situ vaccination“10,11. Such a priming process may enhance the effectiveness of immunotherapies such as ICIs. Preclinical and clinical studies demonstrated that immune responses to RT and ICIs are synergized to improve antitumor activities in various tumor types, including melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer12. Multiple studies in preclinical mouse models of PDAC demonstrated that RT can enhance antitumor response to PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade or dual CTLA-4 and PD-1 blockade, and abscopal effects of RT were observed in these studies13–15. In a phase I clinical trial of patients with metastatic PDAC, SBRT to target lesions in combination with anti-PD-L1 antibody durvalumab or in combination with durvalumab plus anti-CTLA4 antibody tremelimumab showed a moderate therapeutic benefit and an acceptable safety profile with an objective response rate of 5.1%16. In a single-arm phase II clinical trial, RT combined with anti-CTLA4 antibody ipilimumab and anti-PD-1 antibody nivolumab in 25 metastatic, microsatellite-stable PDAC patients resulted in a disease control rate of 20% and objective response rate of 12%17. By far, the largest phase II CheckPAC trial randomized metastatic PDAC patients to receive SBRT to target lesions in combination with nivolumab or with both ipilimumab and nivolumab, demonstrating a higher objective response rate (14.0% vs. 2.4%) in the dual ICI arm than the single ICI arm18. However, as RT is not standard of care for metastatic PDACs and not all the metastatic lesions are candidates for SBRT, the comparable benefit and feasibility of RT in combination with ICIs to systemic therapies remain unknown and would be difficult to assess.

However, RT is still considered to be a standard of care for LAPC, and thus represents an appealing indication to pursue for RT in combination with ICIs. However, prior phase II studies do not show the benefit of anti-PD-1 antibody pembrolizumab being added to RT for borderline resectable PDACs19, and our preclinical data suggest that anti-PD-1 antibody in combination with RT alone would not be sufficient to induce Teffs14. RT can lead to an in situ cancer vaccination effect, which, however, may be associated with inadequate tumor antigen release, insufficient antigen presentation, and immunosuppressive TME. Recent advances in cancer vaccine focus on mRNA-based platforms20 and delivery technologies such as lipid nanoparticles, hydrogels, scaffolds and polymeric nanoparticles21. They show promise in clinical trials for both immunologically “hot” and “cold” tumors, including PDAC, particularly when administered in a minimal disease setting to prevent the recurrence22–24. Combination strategies to improve the efficacy of cancer vaccines include ICIs, cytokines, and chemotherapy25.

We have previously demonstrated that a granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor-secreting allogenic PDAC vaccine (GVAX) administered as a neoadjuvant therapy induced a robust tumor infiltration of Teffs and other immune cells, which formed tertiary lymphoid aggregates26–28. Addition of anti-PD-1 antibody to GVAX27,28 as neoadjuvant therapy for resectable PDACs decreased the quantity of PD-1 + CD8+ and PD-1 + CD4 + T-cells, supporting the presence of the therapeutic effect of anti-PD-1 antibody. Therefore, we developed a single-center, single-arm, phase II clinical trial J15237 (NCT02648282) to test the combination of GVAX, anti-PD-1 antibody pembrolizumab, and SBRT following induction chemotherapy for LAPC patients29. We first reported the correlative studies of this clinical trial, showing that this radioimmunotherapy combination drives TME to feature several antitumor immune response characteristics, including enhanced Teffs infiltration, that are associated with longer survival30. Moreover, we found that adding SBRT to the combination of anti-PD-1 antibody and GVAX shortens the distances from PD-1 + CD8 + T cells to tumor cells and to PD-L1+ myeloid cells30.

Here, we provide the first comprehensive report on the safety and efficacy data of this clinical trial. The data showed that the combination of immunotherapy and RT for stage III PDAC is safe and, compared to the historical control cohort, significantly prolongs the distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) among the surgically explored patients or surgically resected patients.

sec.title: Demographics and clinicopathologic characteristics
sec.p: From July 18th, 2016, to December 14th, 2020, 58 patients with LAPC who met the eligibility criteria were enrolled in the study (Figs. 1 and 2). Of the enrolled patients, 54 were considered evaluable for disease response after receiving two cycles of the combination treatment of cyclophosphamide, GVAX and pembrolizumab, SBRT and had one follow-up scan. These patients had a mean age of 64.2 years (range: 42.0−84.0), and 46.3% were female (Table 1). The majority of patients (88.9%) had a poorly or moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Of the 54 evaluable subjects, 35 subjects (64.8%) were deemed to have potentially resectable PDAC following two cycles of study treatments and subsequently underwent explorative laparotomy (Table 2), including 24 subjects who underwent R0/R1 resections (44.4% of total evaluable subjects) and 11 subjects who were explored and found unresectable. Out of the 11 explored, but unresected patients, 8 had peritoneal carcinomatosis, and 3 had locally advanced unresectable diseases (Table 2). There was no difference in the rate of resectability whether induction chemotherapy was FOLFIRINOX or Gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel.

caption.title: J15237 study treatment schema.
caption.p: Eligible patients with LAPC received the first priming treatment of at least 4 to 8 28-day cycles of Folfirinox or Gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel-based therapy. Screening and baseline procedures for enrollment are done 2–5 weeks after the last dose of chemotherapy. In weeks 2–7, the EUS fiducial placement and simulation scan are done. Patients then received the two cycles of the intradermal administration of GVAX in combination with cyclophosphamide and pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor. Patients also receive an SBRT initiation during the second cycle of the combined immunotherapy. Participants who were then deemed potentially surgical resectable underwent surgical exploration. Subsequently, all participants who were resected and the persistent LAPC received two cycles of standard of care (SOC) chemotherapy. The eligibility was reconfirmed after SOC chemotherapy to resume a 3-week cycle of six additional cycles of combined immunotherapy or until development of distant metastasis. The treatment schema involved a 3-week cycle, consisting of IV infusion of 200 mg/m2 of cyclophosphamide in 100 ml NS over 30 minutes and pembrolizumab 200 mg IV over 30 minutes on Day 1 and six intradermal injections of Gof VAX on Day 2, followed by SBRT administered from Days 1 to 5 of the second treatment cycle. Enrollment occurred from July 18th, 2016, to December 14th, 2020, with follow-up data available until June 1st, 2022. Patients who remained free of distant metastasis after their 8 cycles of the combined immunotherapy had the option to enroll for nine additional doses of pembrolizumab and four additional doses of cyclophosphamide/GVAX every 6 months.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: At the median follow-up time of 19.6 months (mo), median DMFS from first immunotherapy was 9.8 mo (95% CI: 6.3, 19.4) (Fig. 3a) and that of surgically explored patients was 10.2 mo (95% CI: 7.4, 26.3) (Fig. 3b). Median DMFS among those patients who underwent R0/R1 resection was 20.3 mo (95% CI:10.2, NA) (Fig. 3c). In contrast, those who were explored, but did not undergo resection due to presence of peritoneal disease or persistent locally advanced unresectable disease had a median DMFS of 2.4 mo (95% CI:2.4, NA) (Fig. 3d). However, two patients with persistent locally advanced unresectable diseases had a DMFS > 20 months.

The date of death would be considered a DMFS event for patients who died within three months of the last scan, indicating there had been no recurrence.

sec.p: Median OS from the starting date of the immunotherapy among 54 evaluable patients was 21.8 mo (95% CI:13.6, 29.7) (Fig. 4a) and that of surgically explored patients was 27.9 mo (95% CI:17.3, 59.8) (Fig. 4b). Among the patients who underwent R0/R1 resection, median OS of 29.7 mo (95% CI:23.1, NA) (Fig. 4c). In contrast, those surgically explored, but who did not undergo resection had a median OS of 12.1 mo (95% CI:10.9, NA) (Fig. 4d). Median time from the start of immunotherapy to surgical exploration was 75.5 days (95% CI: 71.0, 86.0); and that from the end of immunotherapy to surgical exploration was 53.0 days (95% CI, 50.0, 63.0). Thus, there was no significant delay in surgical exploration due to immunotherapy. Median time from the demonstration of metastasis till death was 5.06 mo (95% CI:3.35, 8.47) in the entire J15237 cohort, 3.63 mo (95% CI: 0.92, 12.32) in the resected cohort, and 6.03 mo (95% CI: 3.91, 9.60) in the unresected cohort, suggesting that once patients developed metastasis, the survival time would be short regardless of the resection status.

sec.p: Median OS from the time of initial diagnosis among 54 evaluable patients was 28.2 mo (95% CI:20.4, 36.7) (Fig. 4e) and that of surgically explored patients was 35.6 mo (95% CI:25, NA) (Fig. 4f). Among those surgically explored, the patients who underwent R0/R1 resection had a median OS of 36.7 mo (95% CI:28.8, NA) (Fig. 4g). In contrast, those surgically explored, but who did not undergo resection had a median OS of 19.7 mo (95% CI:17.2, NA) (Fig. 4h). The difference between median OS from the time of initial diagnosis and that from the starting date of the immunotherapy reflects the length of induction chemotherapy, which appears to be similar among different subgroups of patients according to resectability.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: All patients experienced mild reactions (Grade 1-2) at the vaccine injection site. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events primarily involved immune-related adverse events that occurred in 12% of patients, including pneumonitis (n = 1), diabetic ketoacidosis from immune-related pancreatitis (n = 1), abdominal pain and colitis (n = 1), elevated liver enzymes (n = 2), nephritis (n = 1), and rash (n = 1) (Table 4). Elevated liver enzymes were not associated with clinical evidence of hepatitis. No delay of surgery due to treatment-related adverse events or unexpected postoperative complications was noted. Among patients eligible for surgical resection, one died of cholangitis prior to surgery, unrelated to study treatments.

sec.title: Comparison between the J15237 cohort and the historical control cohort
sec.p: To address the effect of neoadjuvant immunotherapy, J15237 patients were also compared to a historical control cohort of LAPC patients from the Johns Hopkins Pancreatic Cancer Registry during the time when J15237 was enrolling. 68 patients with LAPC were identified using the same eligibility criteria as J15237. Of these 68 patients, 45 were deemed to have potentially explorable PDAC following the neoadjuvant chemotherapy and SBRT and subsequently underwent explorative laparotomy. These 45 surgically explored historical control patients had a mean age of 65.3 years (range: 48.7–79.0), and 44.4% were female (Supplemental Table 1). During laparotomies, 42 subjects underwent R0/R1 resections. Of the 42 patients who underwent R0/R1 resections, 81.0% had R0 resections; 38.1%, 28.6%, 21.4% and 11.9% had pT-stage 1, 2, 3, or 4 diseases, respectively; and 59.5% had no regional nodal involvement (Supplemental Table 2). Common variables between the J15237 and historical control cohorts are comparable (Supplemental Tables 3 and 4). DMFS and OS were obtained from the explored historical control cohort of 45 patients due to a lack of consistent follow-up on those patients who did not undergo surgical exploration.

The DMFS among the surgically explored patients in the J15237 clinical trial was significantly longer than that in the historical control cohort (median DMFS 10.2 vs. 9.5 mo, p < 0.001) (Fig. 3b) with an HR of 0.34 (95% CI: 0.19, 0.61; Table 5), stratified by resectability. The DMFS among the resected patients in the J15237 clinical trial was significantly longer than that in the historical control cohort (median DMFS 20.3 vs. 10.2 mo, p = 0.002) (Fig. 3c) with an HR of 0.40 (95% CI: 0.22, 0.72; Table 5).

sec.p: The OS from the starting date of immunotherapy and that from the date of initial diagnosis among the surgically explored patients in the J15237 clinical trial was not significantly different, but demonstrates a trend of improvement, compared to that from the starting date of SBRT and that from the date of initial diagnosis in the historical control cohort (median OS 27.9 vs. 26.0 mo, p = 0.338 and 35.6 vs. 33.1 mo, p = 0.426, respectively) (Fig. 4b, f) with an HR of 0.77 (95% CI:0.45, 1.32, p = 0.340) and an HR of 0.80 (95% CI:0.47, 1.38, p = 0.427), respectively, stratified by resectability (Table 5). The OS from the starting date of immunotherapy and that from the date of initial diagnosis among the resected patients in the J15237 clinical trial was similarly not significantly different, but demonstrates a trend of improvement, compared to that from the starting date of SBRT and that from the date of initial diagnosis in the historical control cohort (median OS 29.7 vs. 26.1 mo, p = 0.2 and 36.7 vs. 34.1 mo, p = 0.284, respectively) (Fig. 4c, g) with an HR of 0.68 (95% CI:0.37, 1.23, p = 0.203) and an HR of 0.72 (95% CI:0.39, 1.32, p = 0.286), respectively (Table 5).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To our knowledge, this is the largest study of testing the combination of immunotherapy and RT for stage III PDAC. Other published clinical trials of immunotherapy for PDACs were summarized in Supplemental Table 5. Compared to the historical control cohort, the DMFS among the surgically explored patients or surgically resected patients in this J15237 clinical trial was significantly prolonged. More impressive is the DMFS of 20.3 months among the surgically resected patients in the J15237 clinical trial compared to 10.2 months in the historical control cohort. Although the clinical trial did not meet the primary endpoint of prolonging DMFS to 13.6 months in the entire cohort, the study treatment strategy may benefit the patients who underwent the surgical resection. On another hand, the combination of GVAX and pembrolizumab in combination with SBRT did not appear to offer a benefit for those who did not undergo surgical resection.

The median DMFS of 9.8 mo among 54 evaluable patients in this study is comparable to the median progression-free survival of 10.7 mo reported in the prior study of SBRT for LAPCs31. Median OS from the starting date of the immunotherapy among 54 evaluable patients was 21.8 mo, and that of surgically explored patients was 27.9 mo. These results are compared more favorably than the median OS of 18.0 mo reported in the prior studies of SBRT with or without heat-killed mycobacterium vaccinations for LAPCs31,32. Those surgically explored, but who did not undergo resection, had a median OS of 19.7 mo, which is also compared more favorably than that reported in our previously published cohort of LAPCs following standard of care induction chemotherapy and radiation (median OS, 16.3 mo)2.

The study treatment strategy tested in J15237 appeared to benefit the patients who underwent the surgical resection. One possibility is that SBRT plays an abscopal effect in combination with GVAX and pembrolizumab. Our results suggested that the systemic anti-tumor effect from the combination of GVAX/pembrolizumab/SBRT would provide more benefits to those with minimal residual disease and prevent the development of distant metastases, while the combination is not more effective than SBRT itself on the primary tumors. Thus, the future development should focus on further improving the resectability of LAPCs.

The efficacy result presented in this study is consistent with our recently published correlative studies of this clinical trial30 showing that a positive correlation between the infiltration of GZMB + CD8+ cytotoxic Teffs and OS in patients who underwent surgical resection was not observed in patients still with unresectable diseases after the study treatment, suggesting that GVAX/pembrolizumab-induced Teffs infiltration did not transform into an improved clinical outcome in unresected PDACs. In contrast, a decrease in the M1/M2-like tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) ratio, due to an increase of M2-like TAMs, was significantly associated with OS < 2 years in unresected PDACs30. Therefore, M2-like TAMs in PDACs that remained unresected following neoadjuvant treatments may account for the lack of benefit from the combination of GVAX and pembrolizumab. Targeting TAM may improve the resectability of LAPCs and/or may improve the outcome of LAPCs that remain unresectable following neoadjuvant treatments. Based on these findings, we recently completed a clinical trial of a CCR2/CCR5 dual antagonist that targets TAMs in combination with nivolumab with or without GVAX following mFOLFIRINOX-based induction chemotherapy and SBRT for LAPCs (NCT03767582). The endpoints of this new clinical trial are still being analyzed.

This study has a few limitations. This study did not use the trend of CA19-9 as a surrogate marker for tumor responses to the study treatment, although we collected the results before and after Cycle 1 of immunotherapy. We do not anticipate that the change of CA19-9 before and after Cycle 1 of immunotherapy would correlate with the treatment response to radioimmunotherapy because of the short interval between the two tests and because of rising CA19-9 secondary to radioimmunotherapy-induced inflammatory reaction. Another limitation of this single-arm trial is the potential for patient selection bias, as it enrolled patients who remained locally advanced after 4–8 months of chemotherapy or had responded to chemotherapy; thus, they were pre-selected rather than those newly diagnosed with LAPC. To mitigate the potential impact of patient selection bias on treatment effect assessment, we compared the outcomes of the J15237 cohort with a historical control cohort that met the same eligibility criteria as the J15237 tria,l with matched patient characteristics and also received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with either mFOLFIRINOX or Gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel for a minimum of 4 months and a maximum of 8 months followed by SBRT. Although the difference in OS between the J15237 cohort and the historical control cohort does not reach statistical significance, there is a numerical improvement in OS, particularly among the resected patients in the J15237 cohort. Future evaluations of DMFS and OS on those who undergo surgical resection are warranted by conducting a randomized study with a larger sample size. Nevertheless, the treatment strategy would need to be further improved to enhance the resectability of LAPCs and the response of unresected tumors to the treatment. In future studies for LAPC, the radioimmunotherapy strategy shall include macrophage-targeting agents as proposed above.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This is a single-center, single-arm, phase II clinical trial of patients with LAPC seen at the Johns Hopkins Hospital (Baltimore, Maryland, USA). Eligible patients with LAPC received treatments of GVAX administered intradermally in combination with immunomodulatory doses of cyclophosphamide and anti-PD-1 antibody (pembrolizumab), and SBRT prior to the surgical evaluation (Fig. 1). If participants were deemed potentially surgical candidates, surgical exploration would be performed. Regardless of whether tumors were resected, participants without metastatic disease would further receive the standard of care chemotherapy for two 4-week cycles followed by maintenance therapy with every 3-week cycles of cyclophosphamide, GVAX, and pembrolizumab. Further information regarding the trial design can be found on clinicaltrials.gov.

sec.title: Study population and evaluable patients
sec.p: The target population for this study was patients with LAPC. Key eligibility requirements at time of enrollment included the following: age above 18 years old; confirmed diagnosis of PDAC; deemed to have a locally advanced tumors by multidisciplinary tumor board review of the radiographic studies at the time of initial diagnosis according to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network guideline; who remained without metastatic disease after receiving at least 4-four week cycles, but no more than 8-four week cycles of FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel based chemotherapy; no known secondary malignancies within five years of diagnosis of pancreatic cancer; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status ≤1; no radiographic evidence of metastases; no serious autoimmune disease requiring treatment with systemic corticosteroids; adequate organ function. All patients who met trial criteria were offered the trial without any anticipated bias. As pre-planned in the clinical protocol, patients evaluable for efficacy endpoints were those who received at least the first two cycles of GVAX and pembrolizumab in combination with a full course of SBRT. All subjects who received the first dose of study therapy were evaluable for safety endpoints.

sec.title: Outcomes/endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoint was DMFS. A sample size of 54 evaluable subjects provided 80% power to detect an increase in the median DMFS from 7.7 months based on historical data to 13.6 months (corresponding to an HR of 0.57), using a one-sample test with a two-sided type I error of 0.05. Secondary endpoints included the clinical endpoints of OS, subsequent surgical resectability, and pathologic response. Quality of life was assessed via the EORTC QLQ-C30/Pan26 (v3.0) questionnaire and will be presented in another study. As described above, exploratory correlative studies were also conducted and published elsewhere30.

sec.title: Enrollment
sec.p: From July 18th, 2016, to December 14th, 2020, 58 patients were enrolled. The data reported herein reflect follow-up through June 1st, 2022.

sec.title: Treatment schema and assessments
sec.p: Participants underwent baseline biopsies at the time of fiducial placement for SBRT. Study treatments were given on a 21-day cycle, with cyclophosphamide 200 mg/m2 IV and pembrolizumab 200 mg IV administered on Day 1 and GVAX intradermally injected equally into six intradermal areas in both lower limbs and the non-dominant upper limb, as described previously, administered on Day 2. Linac-based SBRT was given as previously described33 with 5 fractions of 6.6 Gy from Days 1 to 5 of cycle 2 (Fig. 1). After two cycles, clinical resectability was determined by consensus of the multidisciplinary team. Tumors deemed resectable proceeded for surgical exploration. If tumors remained clinically unresectable, participants underwent repeat biopsy. After resection or biopsy, all patients without metastatic disease received another two 4-week cycles of either FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/Nab-paclitaxel-based treatments at the discretion of their primary oncologists. Following these post-SBRT chemotherapy, participants who remained metastasis-free would continue to receive every 21-day cycle of cyclophosphamide, GVAX, and pembrolizumab for 1 year, followed by maintenance nine cycles of pembrolizumab every three weeks with concurrent every six-month cyclophosphamide/GVAX for four doses if response/tolerance persisted (Fig. 1).

Patients were assessed for local or distant disease recurrence by CT scans prior to enrollment, following recovery from definitive surgery, and then every 3 cycles while on study treatment. Toxicities were graded using CTCAE v.4.0. Postoperative complications within 30 days of surgery were graded by the Clavien Dindo Criteria.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: DMFS was defined as the time from the start of immunotherapy until the identification of distant metastases on imaging. Individuals were censored with respect to DMFS at the date of last restaging scan if they were alive and had no evidence of metastatic disease. For patients who died within 3 months of the last scan showing no recurrence, the date of death would be counted as an event date of DMFS. OS was defined as the time from the start of immunotherapy until death from any cause. Additional OS from the time of initial diagnoses until death from any cause was also calculated. Individuals were censored with respect to OS at the date of their last known alive. The Kaplan–Meier method was used to summarize DMFS and OS.

sec.title: Historical control cohort generation and analysis
sec.p: This study was initially designed to compare with the historical phase 2 multi-institutional trial evaluating gemcitabine and SBRT as neoadjuvant therapy for LAPCs34; however, since the clinical trial initiation, the neoadjuvant chemotherapy has changed, utilizing more intensive cytotoxic therapy (FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel compared to gemcitabine) for longer time periods (4–8 months pre-RT, compared to historical <6 months). Therefore, for comparison, a historical control cohort was generated, consisting of 45 patients who received definitive pancreatic cancer resection from June 2013 to May 2019 at Johns Hopkins Hospital/Sidney Kimmel Cancer Center. The data cutoff used for the historical control cohort analysis is December 31, 2021. Eligibility criteria for the historical control cohort were the same as the trial: patients with LAPC who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with either mFOLFIRINOX or Gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel followed by SBRT at least 4 months later (Supplemental Fig. 1). The comparisons of patient characteristics and resectability between J15237 cohort and historical control cohort were conducted using Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables and Fisher’ exact tests for binary variables. Stratified log-rank tests, stratified by resectability, were performed for DMFS and OS to compare J15237 vs. historical control cohorts, and the difference was quantified by hazard ratio estimate from Cox regression stratified by resectability. According to available data, there is no obvious difference in the time from the diagnosis to the initiation of chemotherapy between the J15237 cohort and the historical control cohort. Among the surgically explored patients, we compared the OS from the starting date of immunotherapy in the J15237 trial to that from the starting date of SBRT in the historical control cohort, as well as the OS since the date of initial diagnosis between them. Subgroup comparisons were performed by resected and unresected patients, for surgically explored patients. Tests were two-sided, and p-values less than 0.05 were considered to indicate statistical significance.

sec.title: Ethics and compliance
sec.p: The study (J15237) was approved by the Johns Hopkins Institutional Review Board and Institutional Biosafety Committee, as well as the Food and Drug Administration Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research and the National Institutes of Health Recombinant DNA Advisory Committee (NCT02648282). The trial was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki and the Good Clinical Practice guidelines of the International Conference on Harmonization. Informed, written consent was obtained from all patients.
